titulo_es: Emphasis with do and with auxiliaries
descripcion_es: Emphatic do/does/did in affirmative sentences (I do agree, She did call) and stressed auxiliaries to contradict or insist.
resumen: In English you can strengthen a statement by adding do, does or did before the verb in the present or past simple, or by stressing the auxiliary if there already is one. It is used to contradict, insist, concede or show enthusiasm.

filas: I HAVE finished! (stress on the auxiliary)

explicacion.texto: After emphatic do/does/did the verb is in the infinitive without to: She did call (not “did called”), He does know (not “does knows”). In speech, the auxiliary is pronounced with stress; in Spanish we usually translate it with “sí”, “de verdad”, “claro que” or “la verdad es que”.

items: To contradict: “You didn't lock the door.” “I did lock it!” (es: ¡Que sí la cerré!).
To concede before a but: I do understand your point, but I disagree.
To express enthusiasm or sincerity: I do hope you can come.
With other auxiliaries (be, have, will, can) it is enough to stress them: “You're not listening.” “I AM listening!”.
In formal writing it is useful for qualifying a statement: The data do suggest a slowdown, although…

ejemplos.frase: I do apologise for the delay.
ejemplos.traduccion: Le pido sinceras disculpas por el retraso.

ejemplos.frase: "You forgot my birthday." "I did remember! I just didn't have time to call."
ejemplos.traduccion: «Te olvidaste de mi cumpleaños.» «¡Que sí me acordé! Es que no tuve tiempo de llamar.»

ejemplos.frase: She does look tired, doesn't she?
ejemplos.traduccion: La verdad es que parece cansada, ¿no?

ejemplos.frase: Do help yourself to some cake.
ejemplos.traduccion: Sírvete pastel, por favor, no te cortes.

ejemplos.frase: I didn't buy a new car, but I did buy a new bike.
ejemplos.traduccion: No me compré un coche nuevo, pero sí una bici nueva.

ejemplos.frase: We do need to discuss the budget before Friday.
ejemplos.traduccion: De verdad que tenemos que hablar del presupuesto antes del viernes.

errores_hispanohablantes.nota: After does the verb is in the infinitive, without -s.
After did the verb is in the infinitive, not in the past.
The emphatic Spanish “sí” is translated with do, not with yes.

ejercicios.enunciado: Complete with do, does or did for emphasis.
ejercicios.frase: "You don't like jazz, do you?" "I ___ like it, actually!"
ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the rule in the table in Rules and key points: in the present simple, emphasis is formed with do + infinitive. The clue is the contradiction: the other speaker claims you don't like jazz and the reply denies it, reinforced by actually. The subject is I, so the auxiliary is do (not does), followed by like in the infinitive: I do like it.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Present simple, first person: do + infinitive.
ejercicios.traduccion: «No te gusta el jazz, ¿verdad?» «¡Pues sí que me gusta, la verdad!»

errores_previstos.explicacion: Does is for the third person singular; with I we use do.
It is the calque of Spanish “sí que me gusta”; in English yes cannot go before the verb, emphasis is made with do.
Did would mark the past; the conversation is about present likes, in the present.

ejercicios.enunciado: Complete with do, does or did for emphasis.
ejercicios.frase: "Did she phone you?" "Yes, she ___ phone, but I was out."
ejercicios.explicacion: This is the past simple rule from the table: did + infinitive. The clue is the question in the past (Did she phone you?) and the concession with but that follows: the answer insists that the call took place. The auxiliary did already marks the past, so phone is in the infinitive (she did phone, not “she did phoned”).
ejercicios.traduccion: «¿Te llamó?» «Sí, sí que llamó, pero yo no estaba.»

errores_previstos.explicacion: Does is present; the question and the context (I was out) are in the past, so did is required.
Do is present and also does not agree with she; the past is marked with did.

ejercicios.enunciado: Complete with do, does or did for emphasis.
ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the rule in the table for the third person present: does + infinitive. The clue is the subject this soup, third person singular, and the enthusiastic tone shown by the exclamation. With does, smell is in the infinitive without -s: This soup does smell good! In Spanish it is translated with an exclamation or with “de verdad”.

errores_previstos.explicacion: With a third person singular subject (this soup) the auxiliary is does, not do.
“This soup is smell good” mixes be with a verb in the infinitive; emphasis in the present simple is made with does.

ejercicios.enunciado: Complete with the correct form of the verb.
ejercicios.frase: He did ___ (try) his best, even if he lost.
ejercicios.explicacion: This is the rule from Rules and key points: after emphatic do/does/did the verb is in the infinitive without to. The clue is did before the gap: the past is already marked on the auxiliary, so try cannot take -ed. The sentence concedes the effort before the contrast with even if he lost, one of the typical uses of emphatic do.
ejercicios.traduccion: Sí que lo intentó de verdad, aunque perdiera.

errores_previstos.explicacion: Did already expresses the past; repeating it on the verb (did tried) is an incorrect double conjugation.
After do, does or did the infinitive has no to.
Did is not followed by the -ing form, but by the infinitive without to.

ejercicios.frase: I ___ hope you'll be able to come to the wedding.
ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the use from the list in Rules and key points “to express enthusiasm or sincerity: I do hope you can come”. The clue is the subject I with a verb of wishing in the present: the emphatic auxiliary is do. It is the natural way of saying “I really hope that…” (es: “espero de verdad que…” or “ojalá puedas venir”).
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Emphasis in the present with I: do.
ejercicios.traduccion: Espero de verdad que puedas venir a la boda.

por_opcion.do: Correct: I do hope expresses a sincere wish in the present; do agrees with I.
por_opcion.am: Incorrect: “I am hope” mixes be with a verb in the base form; be cannot be used to emphasise a lexical verb.
por_opcion.does: Incorrect: does is for the third person singular; with I we use do.
por_opcion.did: Incorrect: did would place the wish in the past, but this is a present hope about a future wedding.

ejercicios.frase: She does ___ a lot of money, but she's always broke.
ejercicios.explicacion: This is the rule that after does the verb is in the infinitive without -s. The clue is does, which already carries the third person present marking: that is why the main verb stays in the base form (earn). The sentence is a concession before but, another typical use: you admit that he earns a lot in order to contrast it afterwards.
ejercicios.traduccion: Gana mucho dinero, la verdad, pero siempre está sin blanca.

por_opcion.earn: Correct: does + infinitive without -s; does already marks the third person.
por_opcion.earns: Incorrect: repeating the -s after does is the classic double agreement error (does earns).
por_opcion.earned: Incorrect: does cannot be followed by a past tense or a past participle.
por_opcion.to earn: Incorrect: the infinitive after do, does or did has no to.

ejercicios.enunciado: Choose the most natural answer to contradict.
ejercicios.frase: "You didn't send the email." "I ___ send it! Check your spam folder."
ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the “to contradict” use from the list: did + infinitive to deny a past fact. The clue is the accusation in the past simple (You didn't send) and the reply that denies it. Did send is equivalent to Spanish “¡que sí lo envié!”. Have sent would also be a possible tense in other contexts, but here the original sentence is in the past simple and have send is not grammatical.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Contradicting a past fact: did + infinitive.
ejercicios.traduccion: «No enviaste el correo.» «¡Que sí lo envié! Mira en la carpeta de spam.»

por_opcion.did: Correct: did send contradicts a past fact expressed in the past simple.
por_opcion.do: Incorrect: do is present; sending is a past event that the other speaker has denied in the past.
por_opcion.have: Incorrect: with have the past participle would be needed (I have sent it); “I have send it” is not grammatical.

ejercicios.frase: My brother does plays the guitar very well.
respuestas: My brother does play the guitar very well.
ejercicios.explicacion: This is the rule from Rules and key points: after does the verb is in the infinitive, without -s. The clue is does, which already marks the third person present; that is why plays must become play. It is the same error the card shows in “He does knows the answer”.
ejercicios.traduccion: Mi hermano toca muy bien la guitarra, de verdad.

errores_previstos.respuesta: My brother does plays the guitar very well.
errores_previstos.explicacion: This is the uncorrected sentence: after does the verb takes no -s.

errores_previstos.respuesta: My brother do play the guitar very well.
errores_previstos.explicacion: The -s has been removed from the verb, but also from does: with my brother the auxiliary must be does.

errores_previstos.respuesta: My brother does playing the guitar very well.
errores_previstos.explicacion: After does comes the infinitive without to, not the -ing form.

ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the rule that after did the verb is in the infinitive: did already marks the past. The clue is did before enjoyed; keeping the -ed ending means marking the past twice. The correct form is did enjoy.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: After did, infinitive; did already marks the past.
ejercicios.traduccion: Disfrutamos mucho del concierto, de verdad.

errores_previstos.explicacion: This is the uncorrected sentence: after did the verb takes no -ed.
It mixes a present auxiliary with a past form; for emphasis in the past we use did + enjoy.
After did comes the infinitive without to, not the -ing form.

ejercicios.frase: I don't speak German, but I do understanding it.
respuestas: I don't speak German, but I do understand it.
ejercicios.explicacion: This is the rule from Rules and key points: after do the verb is in the infinitive without -ing. The clue is the contrast with but: one thing is denied (I don't speak it) and the other is stated emphatically (I do understand it), the equivalent of Spanish “pero sí”. Do understand is the correct form; understanding is not possible after do.
ejercicios.traduccion: No hablo alemán, pero sí lo entiendo.

errores_previstos.respuesta: I don't speak German, but I do understanding it.
errores_previstos.explicacion: This is the uncorrected sentence: after do comes the infinitive, not the -ing form.

errores_previstos.respuesta: I don't speak German, but I yes understand it.
errores_previstos.explicacion: It is the calque of Spanish “pero sí lo entiendo”; yes cannot go before the verb, emphasis is made with do.

errores_previstos.respuesta: I don't speak German, but I do understands it.
errores_previstos.explicacion: With I there is no -s; after do the verb is in the base form: understand.

ejercicios.enunciado: Rewrite the sentence with emphatic do, does or did.
respuestas: She does look like her mother.
ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the rule in the table for the third person present: does + infinitive. The clue is the subject she and the verb looks, in the present simple: when does is added, the -s moves to the auxiliary and the verb stays in the base form (look). So She does look like her mother insists on the resemblance.
ejercicios.traduccion: Sí que se parece a su madre.

errores_previstos.respuesta: She does looks like her mother.
errores_previstos.explicacion: Double third person marking: does already carries the -s, so the verb is look.

errores_previstos.respuesta: She do look like her mother.
errores_previstos.explicacion: With she the auxiliary is does, not do.

errores_previstos.respuesta: She is look like her mother.
errores_previstos.explicacion: Be cannot be used to emphasise a lexical verb; the form is does look.

ejercicios.enunciado: Rewrite the sentence with emphatic do, does or did.
ejercicios.frase: I warned you about the traffic.
respuestas: I did warn you about the traffic.
ejercicios.explicacion: This is the rule in the table for the past simple: did + infinitive. The clue is warned, past simple: when did is added, the verb goes back to its base form (warn). The sentence has the reproachful nuance of “I did warn you!”, a very frequent use of emphatic did.

errores_previstos.respuesta: I did warned you about the traffic.
errores_previstos.explicacion: Double past marking: did already expresses the past, the verb is in the base form (warn).

errores_previstos.respuesta: I do warn you about the traffic.
errores_previstos.explicacion: Do is present; the original sentence is in the past (warned), so the auxiliary must be did.

ejercicios.enunciado: Rewrite the sentence with emphatic do, does or did.
ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the present simple rule: do + infinitive. The clue is the subject they and the verb need in the present: the emphatic auxiliary is do and need is already in the base form. They do need more staff reinforces the need, as in a report that insists on a piece of data.

errores_previstos.explicacion: Does is only for the third person singular; with they we use do.
After do the verb is in the base form, without -s.
Really also adds emphasis, but the exercise explicitly asks for emphatic do.

respuestas: I do agree with your point
ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the general rule on the card: emphatic do goes before the main verb. The order is subject (I), do, verb (agree) and its complement with with (with your point). It is a very useful formula in debates, often followed by a concession (“I do agree with your point, but…”).
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Emphatic do before the main verb.
ejercicios.traduccion: Estoy totalmente de acuerdo con lo que planteas.

errores_previstos.respuesta: I agree do with your point
errores_previstos.explicacion: Emphatic do always goes before the main verb, not after it.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Do I agree with your point
errores_previstos.explicacion: With do before the subject it becomes a question; emphasis requires the order subject + do + verb.

ejercicios.explicacion: This is the use in the table “Imperative: Do sit down (polite invitation)”. The clue is please and the imperative form sit down: adding do before the verb turns the order into a kind, insistent invitation. Please can go at the beginning, at the end or between do and the verb, which is why three orders are accepted.

errores_previstos.explicacion: Do cannot separate the verb from its particle; it goes before sit.
Emphatic do goes before the verb, not at the end of the sentence.

descripcion_larga_es: Emphatic do (do, does, did before the verb) and stress on the auxiliary are used in English to insist, contradict, concede before a “but” or show enthusiasm. It is equivalent to Spanish “sí que”, “claro que” or “de verdad”. It is frequent in conversation and useful in formal argument, and Spanish speakers find it difficult because they tend to say “yes” or to conjugate the verb twice.

contexto.que_es: It is the use of do, does or did before the main verb in affirmative sentences in the present or past simple, not to form questions or negatives, but to reinforce what is said. After the auxiliary the verb is in the infinitive without to. If the sentence already has another auxiliary (be, have, can, will), emphasis is achieved by stressing it in pronunciation.
contexto.por_que_importa: It lets you express nuances that Spanish marks with “sí que”, “claro que” or “la verdad es que”, and that cannot be translated with yes in English. It is common when contradicting (“I did lock it!”) and very useful in a debate or a presentation to concede a point before refuting it (I do understand your point, but…). Using it wrongly, with double conjugation (did told), is a very noticeable mistake.
contexto.cuando_se_usa: It is used when replying to a statement or question you want to deny, when insisting on something the other person doubts, when conceding before but or although, to show sincerity or enthusiasm (I do hope…) and in polite invitations with the imperative (Do sit down). The signals are a previous contradiction, an “actually” or a contrast. Where a Spanish speaker would say “yo sí que…”, English uses do.
